newsitem.title: USA: Security tight as Abrego drug case opens in Texas.
newsitem.headline: Security tight as Abrego drug case opens in Texas.

text.p: Jury selection began on Monday amid tight security in the trial of Juan Garcia Abrego, reputed head of a Mexican drug cartel that at one time shipped a third of the cocaine consumed in the United States.

Prosecutors allege that Garcia Abrego headed the notorious Gulf Cartel, which supposedly smuggled billions of dollars of cocaine into the United States from a base in northern Mexico for Colombia's Cali druglords.

He has pleaded not guilty to federal drug trafficking, bribery and money laundering charges and faces up to life in prison if convicted. He sat in the courtroom listening impassively to attorneys questioning jurors about their knowledge of the case.

He was not handcuffed but plainclothes officers from the U.S. Marshall's Service were posted inside and outside the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Ewing Werlein and everyone entering the court had to pass through two metal detectors.

Several members of Garcia Abrego's family attended the hearing but he did not acknowledge them as they entered the courtroom. He was captured on Jan. 14 by a special unit of camouflaged Mexican drug agents who ambushed him on his ranch near the northern Mexico city of Monterrey.

At the time he was on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list of criminals and had a $2 million bounty on his head. A day later, he was flown to Houston for prosecution on a 28-count indictment against him and seven alleged cartel lieutenants.
U.S. and Mexican authorities say he is a U.S. citizen, born in South Texas, but his lawyers say he is a Mexican and was deported to the United States without due process.

Garcia Abrego came from a poor family but rose to become one of Mexico's wealthiest and most powerful men. He allegedly amassed a fortune estimated at $15 billion from drug smuggling and Mexican police last month seized four estates, 28 houses, two warehouses and 89 businesses believed to be owned by him.
U.S. prosecutors also are seeking forfeiture of at least $275 million in cash and property.

Despite speculation he could expose Mexican government corruption and provide details on operations of the Cali cartel, there were no signs Garcia Abrego was cooperating with prosecutors to avoid a possible life sentence.

Prosecutors were basing their case on 51 months of wiretapped telephone conversations, stacks of shipping ledgers and business records and the testimony of convicted drug traffickers willing to trade evidence against Garcia Abrego for reduced sentences, according to court filings.
Jury selection was expected to last several days.
